power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Anhedonia is a core symptom of depression and is associated with greater illness severity and poorer outcomes in young people.
The Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) is a validated 14-item multidimensional measure, but no empirically derived screening threshold exists for the original English-language scale.
To derive a provisional ASA screening threshold in older adolescents and young adults.

In 1199 participants aged 16-25 years recruited in the UK, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses evaluated the ASA against three reference criteria: depressive symptom caseness (Mood and Feelings Questionnaire [MFQ] ≥27), self-reported clinician diagnosis of depression (n = 709) and anhedonia caseness on the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS; n = 433).
Optimal thresholds were identified using the Youden index, and performance was compared across age groups and gender and in a 5-month follow-up subsample (n = 332).
The ASA had excellent discrimination against MFQ caseness (AUC = 0.89, 95% CI 0.87-0.91; optimal threshold 16.5, sensitivity 86%, specificity 77%).
Optimal thresholds were 15.5 against both clinician diagnosis (AUC = 0.74, 95% CI 0.70-0.79; sensitivity 88%, specificity 47%) and SHAPS caseness (AUC = 0.83, 95% CI 0.79-0.87).
Discrimination did not differ by age group or gender.
At follow-up, discrimination was outstanding (AUC = 0.94, 95% CI 0.91-0.96), although the optimal threshold was higher (19.5).
Thresholds converged at 15.5-16.5 across reference criteria, supporting a provisional screening threshold of ≥17 for identifying clinically relevant anhedonia in young people.
Replication against structured clinical assessment is needed before this threshold is used diagnostically.

Depression is common among young people: a recent meta-analysis of over 500,000 participants across 29 countries found that approximately one in five children and adolescents report depression or clinically significant depressive symptoms (Lu et al., 2024).

text.text: Early identification and intervention in this age group are therefore critical (Thapar et al., 2012 (Thapar et al., , 2022)).

text.text: Anhedonia, a diminished ability to experience interest or pleasure in typically rewarding activities, is a core symptom of major depressive disorder (MDD) in both DSM-5 and ICD-11 (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2013; World Health Organization [WHO], 2022).

It is highly prevalent among young people with depression, affecting approximately 50-78% (Malhi & Mann, 2018), and is associated with greater illness severity and poorer outcomes (Gabbay et al., 2015).

text.text: Current treatments have limited effectiveness in targeting anhedonia specifically (Cao et al., 2019; Cuijpers et al., 2014), underscoring the need for accurate, developmentally appropriate assessment.
text.formatted: Current treatments have limited effectiveness in targeting anhedonia specifically <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cao et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Cuijpers et al., 2014)</ref>, underscoring the need for accurate, developmentally appropriate assessment.

text.text: The Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) is a 14-item self-report measure grounded in qualitative research on young people's lived experiences of anhedonia (Watson et al., 2020 (Watson et al., , 2021)).
text.formatted: The Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) is a 14-item self-report measure grounded in qualitative research on young people's lived experiences of anhedonia <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Watson et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Watson et al., , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: Items are rated for frequency over the past two weeks on a four-point scale (0 = never to3 = always) and load on three factors: (1) Enjoyment, excitement, and emotional flattening; (2) Enthusiasm, connection, and purpose; and (3) Effort, motivation, and drive.

The ASA showed excellent internal consistency in adolescents aged 11-18 years (α = .93-.94; Watson et al., 2021), and our companion study has extended evidence for its reliability, three-factor structure, and convergent, concurrent and predictive validity to 16-25year-olds (α = .92; test-retest ICC = .69; Demir-Kassem et al., 2026).

text.text: Despite this psychometric support, no empirically derived screening threshold exists for the original English-language ASA.

Two recent studies of a Chinese translation have begun to address this. Ye et al. (2025) identified a threshold of 20.5 for adolescents aged 13-18 years with prominent anhedonia, defined using latent profile analysis, and Kuan et al. (2026) derived thresholds distinguishing adolescents with clinician-diagnosed MDD (21.5) and subthreshold depression (15.5) from healthy controls.

text.text: However, both studies used a translated version of the scale in predominantly early-to mid-adolescent samples.

Without a threshold for the original scale, ASA scores are difficult to interpret in research and clinical settings, limiting its utility relative to measures such as the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS), for which cut-offs have been established in clinical and non-clinical populations (Ho et al., 2024).

text.text: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis is widely used to derive cut-off scores by balancing sensitivity and specificity.
A challenge for anhedonia measures, however, is that there is no gold-standard assessment of clinically significant anhedonia.

Consistent with previous cut-off studies of anhedonia measures (Ho et al., 2024; Kuan et al., 2026), we therefore used depressive symptom caseness on the Mood and Feelings Questionnaire (MFQ; Wood et al., 1995) as the primary reference criterion, with self-reported clinician diagnosis of depression and anhedonia caseness on the SHAPS (Snaith et al., 1995) as secondary criteria.

text.text: Throughout, we use 'clinically relevant anhedonia' to refer to levels of anhedonia associated with clinically significant depressive symptoms, as indexed by these criteria.
The present study aimed to derive a provisional ASA screening threshold for clinically relevant anhedonia in young people aged 16-25 years in the UK.
ROC analyses evaluated the ASA against each reference criterion, with optimal thresholds identified using the Youden index and overall discrimination assessed using the area under the curve (AUC).
We also examined whether discriminatory performance differed by age group and gender, and whether it was maintained in a follow-up subsample assessed approximately five months later.

text.text: The Mood and Feelings Questionnaire (MFQ)
The MFQ is a self-report questionnaire commonly used to screen for depressive symptoms in children and adolescents (Jarbin et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The MFQ is a self-report questionnaire commonly used to screen for depressive symptoms in children and adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Jarbin et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It consists of 33 items rated on a three-point scale (0 = not true,1 = sometimes,2 = true), with higher scores indicating higher levels of depression and is one-dimensional.
Scores range from 0 to 66.

Previous research has reported excellent internal consistency for MFQ scores (Cronbach's alpha .91 to .93), together with evidence of validity and reasonable diagnostic accuracy, with a suggested clinical depression cut-off score of 27 (Thabrew et al., 2018).

text.text: The SHAPS is a self-report tool designed to assess hedonic capacity, or the ability to experience pleasure (Snaith et al., 1995).
text.formatted: The SHAPS is a self-report tool designed to assess hedonic capacity, or the ability to experience pleasure <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Snaith et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: It comprises 14 items, each rated on a four-point scale, covering various aspects of pleasurable experiences in four domains: interest/pastimes, social interaction, sensory experience, and food/drink.
Previous research has reported good internal consistency for SHAPS scores (Cronbach's α = .86).
Originally, it was scored using a dichotomous system with a total score ranging from 0 to 14.

However, we used a four-point Likert scale (items scored 1-4; total scores 14-56, with higher scores indicating greater anhedonia) to better distinguish levels of severity for each item (Franken et al., 2007).

text.text: The ASA was created in collaboration with adolescents experiencing symptoms of depression and anhedonia (Watson et al., 2021).

text.text: Informed by qualitative interviews, the ASA is a multidimensional self-report questionnaire designed to measure anhedonia in adolescents aged 11-18 years.
It covers various components of the anhedonia experience relevant to this age group.
The scale consists of 14 items rated on a four-point scale (0 = never,1 = sometimes,2 = often,3 = always), with higher scores indicating higher levels of anhedonia.
Total scores range from 0 to 42.
The ASA comprises three subscales:  ASA S1-Enjoyment, Excitement, and Emotional Flattening: It has 7 items in the scale and can range from 0 to 21.
 ASA S2-Enthusiasm, Connection, and Purpose: has 3 positively worded items, with scores ranging from 0 to 9.
Items were reverse scored for analysis so that, consistent with the other ASA subscales and the total score, higher scores indicate greater anhedonia.
 ASA S3-Effort, Motivation, and Drive: It has 4 items in the scale and can range from 0 to 12 (see Supplement for scale details).
The scale encompasses both consummatory (enjoyment in the moment) and anticipatory (looking forward to future pleasures) aspects of anhedonia, as well as motivational deficits.
This multidimensional approach provides a more comprehensive assessment of anhedonia in adolescents compared to the SHAPS.
Data were analysed using SPSS 29.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).
Participant demographics were summarized using descriptive statistics, and associations between questionnaire measures were examined using Spearman's rank correlation coefficients.
The discriminatory performance of the Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) and its subscales was evaluated using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.
This analysis was conducted to assess the ability of the ASA to discriminate between participants classified as positive and negative according to each external reference criterion.
The ROC curve plots the true positive rate (sensitivity) against the false positive rate (1specificity) for various threshold settings.
The area under the ROC curve (AUC) was calculated to quantify the overall ability of the scale to discriminate between positive and negative cases.

In general, an AUC of 0.5 suggests no discrimination between participants classified as positive and negative according to the reference criterion, 0.7 to 0.8 is considered acceptable, 0.8 to 0.9 is considered excellent, and more than 0.9 is considered outstanding (Hosmer et al., 2013).

Using the proposed ASA screening threshold of ≥17, 59.8% of participants scored above the threshold including 58.8% in females, 60.3% in males, 55.3% in the 16-19 age group, and 64.1% in the 20-25 age group.
In the group reporting a clinical diagnosis of depression, 84.1% scored above the proposed threshold, compared with 50.9% of those not reporting a diagnosis.

The present study provides empirically derived provisional screening thresholds for the original English-language Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) in a large sample of older adolescents and young adults aged 16-25 years.
Across three external reference criteria at baseline, optimal ASA thresholds were broadly similar, ranging from 15.5 to 16.5.
The MFQbased analysis yielded an optimal threshold of 16.5, whereas both SHAPS-defined anhedonia caseness and self-reported clinician diagnosis of depression yielded thresholds of 15.5.
This convergence suggests that ASA scores around 16-17 may represent a useful provisional screening range.
For practical screening purposes, a score of ≥17 is therefore proposed as the primary candidate threshold.

Together, these findings address a key gap identified in the Introduction: the absence of an empirically derived screening threshold has, until now, limited the ASA's use for identifying individuals with clinically relevant anhedonia symptoms in research and clinical settings.

The strongest evidence for the ASA's discriminatory accuracy came from the MFQ-based analysis, which showed excellent AUC in the full sample and was outstanding in a follow-up sub-sample assessed approximately five months later (AUC = .94), with a similar sensitivity/specificity balance (86%/86% versus 86%/77%).

This consistency across assessments provides further support for the discriminatory performance of the ASA, although the optimal cut-off at follow-up was somewhat higher (19.5 compared with 16.5 at baseline), suggesting some variation in the precise threshold over time.
Discriminatory power was lower when self-reported clinician diagnosis was used as the reference standard (AUC = .74) than for the SHAPS (.83) and MFQ (.89) criteria.
Several factors plausibly explain this pattern.

Clinical diagnosis was based on participant self-report of a prior diagnosis from a health practitioner rather than a structured diagnostic interview conducted as part of the study, introducing measurement noise (recall accuracy, heterogeneity in diagnostic practice, and variation in time since diagnosis or treatment) that would tend to attenuate observed discrimination.
The MFQ, by contrast, is a continuous, validated dimensional measure completed by all participants at the same assessment, providing a cleaner and more proximal benchmark.

The comparison with SHAPS-defined caseness should also be interpreted in light of the conceptual scope of the two measures: as discussed in our companion validation paper (Demir-Kassem et al., 2026), the SHAPS assesses a narrower construct, hedonic capacity, whereas the ASA was developed to capture a broader multidimensional experience of anhedonia encompassing motivation, effort, connection and purpose alongside enjoyment.

text.text: Given this, the excellent discriminatory power observed against SHAPS-defined caseness (AUC = .83) should be interpreted as an estimate of the ASA's discrimination against this specific self-report benchmark.

On balance, and consistent with the convergence across reference criteria, the MFQ-based cut-off of 16.5 supports the proposed screening threshold of ≥17, with the diagnosis-and SHAPSbased cut-offs (both 15.5) offered as converging, secondary benchmarks.

The sensitivity of 88% and relatively low specificity of 47% against reported diagnosis indicate that many participants without an affirmative history of diagnosis nevertheless screened positive; this may reflect elevated symptoms without a reported diagnosis rather than definitive falsepositive screening.

A consistent pattern emerged across all three reference standards and the follow-up sample: the total ASA score performed as well as, or better than, any individual subscale, and the Enthusiasm, Connection, and Purpose subscale (ASA-S2) consistently showed the weakest discriminatory power (AUCs ranging from .63 to .78), while Enjoyment, Excitement, and Emotional Flattening (ASA-S1) and Effort, Motivation, and Drive (ASA-S3) performed comparably to, and at times matched, the total score.

This pattern converges with findings from our companion psychometric validation study (Demir-Kassem et al., 2026), in which the same subscale (ASA-S2) showed the lowest internal consistency and the weakest convergent validity of the three ASA dimensions.

text.text: Taken together, the two studies suggest that the enthusiasm, connection, and purpose items, despite tapping a conceptually important aspect of anhedonia identified in the qualitative work underpinning the ASA, may be somewhat less precise as a discriminator of clinically relevant anhedonia symptoms than the other two dimensions.

This reinforces the recommendation that the total ASA score, rather than individual subscale scores, be used when applying these cut-offs for screening, while the subscale-level findings may still hold value for characterising the specific profile of an individual's anhedonic experience.

Reassuringly, independent-group comparisons indicated no significant differences in AUC by age group (16-19 versus 20-25 years) or gender for any of the three reference standards, supporting similar discriminatory performance across this broader age range and across genders.

Some variation in the optimal cut-off value itself was nonetheless observed between subgroups, particularly for the smaller clinical-diagnosis sub-sample, where the cutoff for the youngest age band diverged more markedly from the other subgroups (age 16-19: ≥23, with only 33 reference-positive cases).

Given the smaller cell sizes involved once the sample was stratified by both diagnosis status and demographic group, this subgroupspecific estimate should be interpreted cautiously and would benefit from replication in a larger, independently diagnosed clinical sample.
Applying the recommended MFQ-based cut-off, approximately 60% of the overall sample scored above the proposed screening threshold , with broadly similar rates across age and gender subgroups.

This is a notably high base rate relative to general population estimates, and likely reflects the characteristics of the recruitment strategy (a convenience sample recruited partly through advertisements referencing mood and wellbeing, and skewed towards female participants) rather than the true population prevalence of clinically significant anhedonia.

Reassuringly, the clinical relevance of the proposed screening threshold is supported by the substantially higher proportion scoring above the threshold among participants reporting a clinical diagnosis of depression (84.1%) compared with those without (50.9%), indicating that the proposed threshold is meaningfully associated with selfreported clinical diagnosis even though the absolute proportions figures in this sample should not be generalised as population estimates.
At ≥17, positive and negative predictive values against MFQ caseness were 84.2% and 79.3%, respectively, and depend on the high reference-positive proportion in this sample.
These findings are broadly consistent with cut-off determination work on other anhedonia measures in adolescent samples, such as the SHAPS (Ho et al., 2024).

text.text: This study has several strengths.

The sample was large and provided substantial power for ROC analysis, cut-offs were derived across three conceptually distinct external reference criteria, and discriminatory performance was examined in a follow-up sub-sample collected approximately five months after baseline.
The examination of AUC differences by age and gender also allowed a direct test of whether a single cut-off is appropriate across this broader age range.
Several limitations should also be acknowledged.
First, an important limitation concerns the nature of the external reference criteria.

The MFQ assesses depressive symptom severity rather than anhedonia specifically and includes symptoms overlapping with anhedonia, the SHAPS is itself a self-report measure of hedonic capacity, and clinical diagnosis was based on participant self-report of receiving a clinical diagnosis rather than directly from a clinician using a structured diagnostic interview, which was not feasible within the large online survey design.

Accordingly, none of these criteria constitutes a gold-standard assessment of current clinically significant anhedonia, and the thresholds identified here should therefore be regarded as provisional screening thresholds.

The use of participant-reported clinical diagnosis may have introduced noise into that reference criterion and may partly explain its comparatively lower AUC; future work should replicate the cut-off analysis in samples with independently verified clinical diagnoses and structured assessments of current anhedonia.
Because the MFQ includes anhedonia-related items, some content overlap with the ASA may inflate the MFQ-based AUC.

Second, the sample was a convenience sample recruited via schools, a university research panel, and online advertisement, was predominantly female, and showed a high overall rate of depressive symptoms; the specific cut-off values, and particularly the prevalence estimates reported here, may not generalise directly to more representative or more diverse clinical populations.

Third, the clinical-diagnosis and SHAPS sub-samples were considerably smaller than the full sample, and the subgroup-level cut-off estimates derived from them (particularly for the youngest age band) should be treated as preliminary.

Finally, although the follow-up sample provided valuable evidence regarding the discriminatory performance of the ASA over time, the follow-up ROC analysis used ASA and MFQ scores collected at the same time point, so it addresses concurrent rather than predictive accuracy.
Future research should examine whether ASA scores above the proposed cut-off predict clinically meaningful outcomes over time, such as treatment response or the subsequent course of depression.

This study provides the first empirically derived provisional screening thresholds for the original English-language Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents, addressing a key barrier to its use in research and clinical practice.

A cut-off of approximately 16.5 on the total ASA score, benchmarked against symptom-based caseness, showed excellent discriminatory performance, with similarly outstanding discriminatory performance observed at follow-up and discriminatory performance did not differ significantly by age or gender within the 16-25year range.
Converging cut-offs derived from self-reported clinician diagnosis and an established anhedonia measure lend further support to a screening threshold in this range.

Combined with evidence from our companion validation study that the ASA's psychometric properties extend reliably into young adulthood, these findings support the use of the ASA, with a provisional screening threshold of ≥17, to identify clinically relevant anhedonia in young people aged 16-25 years who may warrant further assessment.

(2025)  reported a threshold of 20.5 for identifying adolescents aged 13-18 years with prominent anhedonia, defined using latent profile analysis, and<ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kuan et al. (2026)</ref> reported thresholds of 15.5 for subthreshold depression and 21.5 for major depressive disorder versus healthy controls aged 11-22 years.

text.text: The threshold identified here (≥17) closely matches Kuan et al.'s subthreshold-depression threshold (15.5) but is lower than their MDD threshold (21.5) and Ye et al.'s prominent-anhedonia threshold (20.5); these differences may reflect differences in reference criteria (symptom-and self-report-based caseness rather than latent profiles or clinically recruited groups), sample composition, age range, and translation and cultural factors.

The present study is, to our knowledge, the first to derive a screening threshold for the original English-language ASA, and the first to propose one for an older adolescent/young-adult sample spanning 16-25 years.
